sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, match or one word).

questions.q: State True or False: (a) The decay rate of a radioactive element increases with temperature. (b) With artificial radioactivity it is theoretically possible to convert iron into gold.
questions.answer:
(a) False — decay is unaffected by temperature.
(b) True.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) ______ is an effective moderator used in nuclear reactors. (b) Temperature and pressure do not affect a radioactive substance's ______.
questions.answer:

(b) rate of decay (half-life)

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: A radioactive substance decays to 1/32 of its activity in 25 days. Calculate its half-life.
Write two differences between α and β particles.
questions.answer:
(1) α is a helium nucleus with charge +2e; β is an electron with charge −e.
(2) α has greater ionizing power but much less penetrating power than β.

questions.q: Calculate the energy equivalent to 1 atomic mass unit. (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
Mention four characteristics of nuclear force.
questions.answer: (1) It is the strongest force in nature. (2) It is short-range (about 2–3 fm). (3) It is charge-independent (n–n, p–p, n–p alike). (4) It saturates — each nucleon attracts only its neighbours; it is attractive except at very short distances.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: State the law of radioactive decay. Define half-life and decay constant and relate them. Draw the decay curve.
questions.answer:
Law: the rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei, dN/dt = −λN, giving N = N₀e^(−λt).
Decay constant λ: the fraction of nuclei decaying per unit time.
Half-life T½: the time for half the nuclei to decay. Setting N = N₀/2 gives T½ = ln 2/λ = 0.693/λ.
Curve: N against t falls exponentially — N₀, N₀/2, N₀/4 … at equal intervals of T½.

questions.q: Compare α, β and γ radiations.
questions.answer:
Nature: α — helium nuclei (+2e); β — electrons (−e); γ — electromagnetic waves (no charge).
Ionizing power: α greatest, γ least.
Penetrating power: α least (stopped by paper), β moderate (a few mm of aluminium), γ greatest (several cm of lead).
Effect on the nucleus: α lowers A by 4 and Z by 2; β raises Z by 1; γ changes neither.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: What are mass defect and binding energy? Explain the main properties of the nuclear force.
questions.answer:
Mass defect Δm = [Zm_p + (A − Z)m_n] − M_nucleus: the nucleus weighs less than its separate nucleons.
Binding energy = Δm c² (931 MeV per u): the energy needed to break the nucleus into its nucleons. Binding energy per nucleon measures stability; it is highest (about 8.8 MeV) near iron.
Nuclear force: (1) strongest force known; (2) very short range; (3) charge-independent; (4) saturating; (5) attractive except at very small distances, where it is repulsive; (6) it is what holds protons together against their electrostatic repulsion.
